Read 2026-09-22.** `stratum_login` stores the two values in sequence under distinct locks — `*current_linear_template.lock().await = Some(template.clone())` then `*linear_recipient_config.lock().await = Some(config)` (`bin/dwowd/src/rpc/stratum.rs:228`, `:230`) — where `config` is the **login's** own config (it is what `generate_linear_block_template` was called with at `:205`) and the template embeds it. Two concurrent logins can interleave those two writes, leaving one login's template beside the other's config. Nothing detects it: `stratum_submit` reads them separately too (`:465`, `:581`, `:665`, `:704`), there is no generation counter, no joint struct, and no cross-check that the stored template's recipient matches the stored config. The impact is bounded by the design rather than by a guard — there is exactly one stored template and one stored config for the node, so a second miner's login overwrites the first's values and *any* submit is already validated against the newest login — but a torn pair means a submitted block judged against a recipient config its template was not built from. Closing it means storing the template and its config as one lock-protected value, not adding a check. **CLOSED 2026-09-23 by exactly that, in the form the row names.** The three fields are now one: `ActiveTemplate { template, height, recipient_config }`, under one lock, written **only** by `MiningState::store_template` — verified by grep, since that is the whole guarantee (there is no read-time check and none is possible: a torn pair is no longer an expressible state). The recipient is deliberately not an `Option`: a published template always has one, so "template without recipient" cannot be typed. Both submit handlers now take **one snapshot per submission** and read the template, its height, the per-block anchor key, the uncles and the recipient from that clone — the stratum handler previously acquired the lock three times (`:465`, `:590`, `:675`) and this row's own evidence named the consequence: its "the live template moved between login and submit" branch existed only to report the race the bundle removes, and is now unreachable from that handler, kept as a guard with its comment corrected. **Two consequences, both named rather than discovered later.** (i) The merge-mining login used to store the template and the height and **drop** the recipient it had just resolved, so the submit path's next-round template regeneration — guarded on "some config has been stored" — only ever fired on a node that had also served a stratum login; the recipient now travels with the template and the regeneration always runs. (ii) The stale-template check no longer carries its `template_h != 0` escape, because that guard existed for an atomic that read 0 before any template was stored and a snapshot cannot exist without a real height. **Control**: `active_template_tests::test_store_template_publishes_the_triple_as_one_value` publishes a triple, then a *different* triple at a different height with a different per-block recipient, and asserts no field of the first survives — the assertion a publication done in parts fails. **Negative-controlled** by publishing the second triple with the first's recipient retained, which is the old shape's defect class: it fails with two distinct `MiningRecipient` public keys, `0x3f7a2dc6…` against `0x2346b6b9…`, recorded. Also `rpc::mm_rpc` 9/9 green. Pin-neutral: `bin/dwowd` only |
| OBL-C44 | **CLOSED** | A reorg re-admits the disconnected block's transactions to the mempool, as Bitcoin Core does | `H-H10` | M | **OPEN — confirmed by the absence of the operation rather than by reading a broken one. Read 2026-09-22.** The mempool is told about inclusion at five acceptance sites — `bin/dwowd/src/lib.rs:1809`, `rpc/miner.rs:271`, `rpc/mm_rpc.rs:742`, `rpc/stratum.rs:699` and `proto/linear_broadcast.rs:447`, each calling `mp.mark_mined(&tx_hashes)` — and `mark_mined` (`crates/dwow-mempool/src/lib.rs:562-580`) removes those hashes from the pool, persistently (`sled remove`). There is **no inverse**: no `mark_unmined`, no re-insertion path, and neither the reorg driver (`bin/dwowd/src/task/consensus_linear.rs` — which does not mention the mempool at all) nor `CChainState::disconnect_block` (`chain_state.rs`'s only mempool mention is a doc comment on the nullifier set) puts a displaced block's transactions back. So a reorged-away transaction is dropped from the pool and stays gone until its own submitter re-broadcasts it; nothing in the node recovers it. That is a liveness difference from Bitcoin Core — which the row explicitly benchmarks against — rather than a safety one: no double-spend follows, since the nullifier gate is untouched and the transaction remains valid to re-submit. The wire to close it already exists (`mark_mined`'s hashes are computed at each site from `block.transactions`), but the re-admission must happen where the reorg is decided, and that is the daemon's `reorg_to_heavier_chain`, which currently has no mempool handle. **CLOSED 2026-09-23 at the site the row names, by giving it one.** `reorg_to_heavier_chain` and `activate_best_chain` now take `mempool: Option<&MempoolPtr>`; the re-admission happens in `activate_best_chain` **after** the reconnect, so every failure path above it leaves no trace of having been attempted — and the disconnected blocks were already collected there (stashed so a failed reconnect could be logged), which is what makes one location enough. The exclusion set is the row's implicit one made explicit: a displaced block's **coinbase** and **fee collection** are returned to nobody, because both are generated by the block that carried them (the coinbase pays its reward, FeeCollectV1 claims its fee pot and closes its commitment merkle tree). `Transaction::is_fee_collect_tx` is the second half of that, mirroring the existing `is_pow_reward_coinbase_tx` and carrying the same pinned cross-crate note for selector 0x06. **The one design decision worth recording**: a mempool parameter cannot be defaulted in Rust, so the alternative to what landed was threading it through 39 call sites — all of them tests and genesis, none of which has a mempool to give. The path is therefore split in name rather than widened: `accept_block_with_mempool` is the body, `accept_block` is `Some` body called with `None`, both in `block_acceptor.rs`, so no acceptance rule exists twice and each call site says whether it has a handle. The five production entry points — built-in miner, stratum, mm_rpc, miner_rpc and the sync loop's two accept paths — pass one; the P2P broadcast path passes an explicit `None` with the reason stated at the site, and genesis likewise (no mempool exists at genesis). **Control**: `transaction::tests::test_block_generated_tx_classification` pins the exclusion set in both directions (each selector classifies its own call and not the other; neither fires for another contract; neither fires for an empty call list). **Not covered, stated rather than implied**: the re-admission itself has no test — it needs a reorg harness carrying a mempool-admissible *non-coinbase* transaction, and the two halves of that fixture live in different places (`daemon_sync_integration`'s reorg tests build blocks whose only transaction is the coinbase; `mempool_tests.rs` has the transaction fixture but no reorg). Naming it is the honest form of that gap: what is verified is the rule and the call graph, what is not is the runtime effect. The call graph *is* exercised end to end — `daemon_sync_integration` **10 passed / 0 failed** including the three reorg tests, which drive `activate_best_chain` and reorg-to-heavier-chain with `None` and so prove the plumbing did not disturb the reorg — but those runs take the `None` branch, which is exactly the branch that re-admits nothing. Verified with the change: `dwow_chain` 279 passed / 0 failed including the new predicate test, and `dwowd`'s `rpc::`, `mempool_tests` and `active_template_tests` 20 passed / 0 failed |
| OBL-C45 | **PARTLY** | The contracts tree and the supply-chain tree reconcile automatically; no `verify_cumulative_supply()` exists and the `get_cumulative_supply` RPC returns stored state unverified | `H-H11` | M | **OPEN as recorded, with one half of its premise narrowed by what is already enforced. Read 2026-09-22.** The RPC half is exact: `blockchain_get_cumulative_supply` (`bin/dwowd/src/rpc/blockchain.rs:357-380`) reads `chain.supply_chain.get_latest()` — the *stored* entry — and returns its `value_commit`, `blind` and `total_supply` with no recomputation, carrying its own `UNVERIFIED(F3-1): needs cargo test -p dwowd --lib && ./verify_cumulative_supply.sh against a devnet node` tag. No `verify_cumulative_supply()` function exists in the tree at all; `verify_cumulative_supply.sh` is a script nobody calls at runtime, and it compares the stored *plaintext* total against the schedule while disclaiming the commitment half itself (`:70-72`). **What is already enforced, and why the row's first clause is too strong as written**: the two trees are not reconciled globally, but the supply-chain entry is *re-derived and cross-checked at every block* before it is written — `read_cumulative_from_overlay` recomputes `S_H = S_{H-1} + C_base` and rejects the block on any disagreement with the WASM overlay (`block_acceptor.rs:656-689`, `OBL-C25`), and `connect_block` is the only insertion path. So the residual is narrower than "unverified": there is no *read-time* verification and no end-to-end check against the emission schedule outside a script, but every write is step-verified. **PARTLY 2026-09-23: the read-time half is closed, the tree-vs-tree half is not.** `blockchain_get_cumulative_supply` now recomputes the schedule-side total at read time and **fails closed** on a mismatch — the error names both values, rather than returning an `UNVERIFIED` tag beside a `total_supply` a caller cannot distinguish from a verified one. The recomputation is `CumulativeSupplyChain::expected_cumulative_supply`, deliberately the *same name and definition* as `sim/crypto.py:expected_cumulative_supply` and `contrib/model/supply_chain_model.py` — the specification — which is also what `verify_cumulative_supply.sh` compared from the outside, in Python. It is O(height) in reward evaluations, so an operator RPC call and not a per-block path, and it is not memoised: a cache here would be a second piece of stored state to reconcile. **Control**: `test_supply_chain_audit` now cross-checks the schedule-side function against its own store-side audit at every height 1..5 — two independent sums, one over the rewards written into blocks and one over `expected_reward` from the schedule — so an off-by-one that started the sum at 0 or at `h+1` fails there instead of silently mis-reporting supply. The behaviour change is caller-visible and is named rather than implied: a node whose stored total disagrees with the schedule now returns a JSON-RPC **error** where it used to return data, and `verify_cumulative_supply.sh` already handles that branch. What stays open is the row's first clause: the contracts tree and the supply-chain tree are still not reconciled *against each other* anywhere, in Rust or in the script, and nothing in this fix pretends otherwise **— and that first clause now has a *statement*, which is what it was missing.** `proofs/lean/src/DarkFi/Consensus/SupplyReconciliation.lean` states the reconciliation as a composition of three models the layer already had, rather than as a fourth model: `MassBalance.lean`'s `Balanced` (the non-coinbase calls' Pedersen equation), `CoinbaseSplit.lean`'s `accepts` (the coinbase's five equations, whose `accepts_spendable_total` says the miner's note and the uncle notes *together* are the schedule's value — the pins are a share of the same reward, not a second issuance beside it), and `FeeCollect.lean`'s `rule` (the block's fee-collect shape). **The identity**: a block's *net creation of commitment value* — its issuance plus what its non-coinbase calls create, minus what they consume — is the schedule's value at that height (`creation_is_the_reward`), and summed over a chain it is `Σ expected_reward(H)` (`cumulative_creation_is_the_cumulative_supply`), which is the sum the supply-chain tree's own cumulative entry accumulates. **And the fee leg is load-bearing rather than decorative**: `non_coinbase_net_is_the_fee_aggregate` shows that `Balanced` alone fixes the block's net creation at `issuance − Σ fees` — the fees are *parked*, not destroyed — so the identity needs the fee calls to park nothing, and `parked_fees_break_the_identity` is the witness: 150 in against 100 out with a 50-unit aggregate, every value check in both models passing, the contracts tree growing by `base − 50` where the schedule says `base`. **What that exposes is the third leg's weakness, and it is this unit's residue**: `FeeCollect`'s rule is written over FeeV3 *call counts* where `MassBalance` carries the fee *amounts*, so the step from "this block parked an aggregate" to "this block collects" is a bridge **no code check ties**, taken as an explicit hypothesis in `a_block_with_fees_collects` and named there rather than hidden. **Non-vacuity is built from the modules' own witnesses** rather than from new data: `reconciliation_witness` evaluates the identity at `CoinbaseSplit.legalSplit` — that module's accepted split, reused rather than rebuilt — against a call-empty block. **What is unchanged is this row's first clause**: no Rust and no script reads the contracts tree against the supply chain, so `PARTLY` stands, and what moved is that a later reconciliation would be a check *of* a stated property rather than of a paragraph. The level is the specification's (`Commitment` is an integer pair, as in `MassBalance.lean`, so the identity is about values and blinds as integers rather than about `pallas::Point`), and the pot's arithmetic — that the collection's *value* is the aggregate the calls parked — remains the WASM check `FeeCollect`'s note records rather than a hypothesis this module takes |

| OBL-C52 | **CLOSED** | Competing-block dedup hashes use the block hash, not a header serialization | `H-M8` | M | **CLOSED 2026-09-22.** The row understated itself: the two sides of the same set used *different* keys, not merely a different one from the row's preference. The three insert paths keyed on `hash_with_vm` (RandomX over the mining blob) while `take_competing_blocks`, `put_competing_blocks` and `prune_competing` keyed on `blake3(dwow_serialize(header))`, so a take removed an entry that had never been added, the insert's key stayed in the set forever, and a block legitimately re-submitted after being taken as an uncle was **silently dropped as a duplicate** — `CompetingStored` without anything stored, indistinguishable to the caller from success. Both sides now call one `competing_dedup_key`, which is the serialization form: it needs no RandomX VM (so the insert paths lose a hash and a VM lock, and `store_competing_block`'s `pow` gate is now spurious), the three removing paths cannot obtain a VM at all, and `uncles_by_height`'s storage key was already this exact expression — so it is the convention the struct had settled on everywhere except the one place it mattered. `chain_state::tests::competing_block_can_be_re_stored_after_being_taken` is the test, and it was **negative-controlled**: reintroducing the asymmetry at the insert site makes it fail with the row's own name |
| OBL-C53 | **CLOSED** | `consensus.load()` failure is not discarded — a node does not start on silently corrupted state | `H-M9` | M | **CLOSED 2026-09-22.** `PoWConsensus::load` read `target` only `if bytes.len() == 4` and otherwise *skipped it silently*, so a node whose `target` key was damaged started on the **initial target** — a consensus-critical value quietly wrong, with nothing downstream able to tell. The fix draws the distinction the doc comment had already stated and the code did not implement: a value that is **absent** keeps its default (a fresh node has no stored target), and a value that is present but the **wrong length** is corrupt and is now an `Err`. The same class sat in the sibling read — `bytes.chunks_exact(8)` discards a trailing partial chunk, dropping a timestamp without a word — so a `timestamps` value that is not a multiple of 8 is refused too. `consensus::tests::test_load_rejects_corrupt_state_but_allows_absence` covers all three cases: absent loads, each corrupt form errors, and well-formed loads — the third being the positive control that stops a `load` which always errored from satisfying the other two |
| OBL-C54 | **PARTLY** | Template read/write is not racy between stratum login and submit | `H-M10` | M | **PARTLY — the writes are serialised but nothing versions or pairs the template with the login that produced it; one compensating check bounds the damage. Read 2026-09-22, same evidence as `OBL-C43`.** The template is written under its own lock (`stratum.rs:228`) and read under that lock at each site (`:465`, `:581`, `:665`), so no individual read is torn — but the *sequence* is unversioned: `stratum_submit` takes a clone at `:665`, validates the submitted block against it, and a concurrent login may replace it in between, so a submit can be judged against a template that is no longer current. Two things bound this rather than a guard: the template height travels with the template and a stale submit is rejected by `accept_block`'s own height check (the compensation the `OBL-C68` note relies on), and the job cache is single-slot, so "current" is whatever the newest login left. What is absent is what the row asks for — a way to tell whether the template a submit is using is still the one it was issued from, which is the same missing pairing as `C43` (one lock-protected value holding template + config + a generation counter, rather than three independently-written fields). **PARTLY 2026-09-23: the pairing landed, the generation counter did not, deliberately.** The bundle is `C43`'s — one `ActiveTemplate`, one snapshot per submission, both handlers — so the two halves of a submit can no longer come from different rounds; what is *not* added is the counter, and the reason is that a counter's only product here is a **diagnostic**: both ways a replaced template can make a submission wrong are already rejected on their own evidence. A different *height* is refused by the staleness check and again by `accept_block`; a same-height replacement produces a block whose coinbase and merkle root are the new template's while the nonce is the old blob's, which the proof-of-work check rejects — the counter would turn "invalid PoW" into "stale job" in the log, and the row records the residual rather than claiming the diagnostic as a fix. What the pairing *does* change for this row's own concern is that the height and the per-block anchor key now come from the same snapshot the template did, so the stratum handler's "the live template moved between login and submit" branch — the case this row's first clause is about — no longer has a race to detect |
| OBL-C55 | **CLOSED** | `mm_jobs` eviction at capacity is FIFO, not clear-all | `H-M11` | M | **PARTLY — the bulk-clear defect is gone; FIFO is not implemented, and the code says so itself while its neighbouring comment says the opposite. Read 2026-09-22.** `mm_rpc.rs:330-343`: `MAX_MM_JOBS = 100`, and at capacity a **single** entry is removed (`if let Some(evicted) = mm_jobs.keys().next().cloned() { mm_jobs.remove(&evicted); }`) before the new job is inserted — so the bulk `clear()` this row was filed against is gone, which is the half that mattered. **FIFO is not what happens**: `mm_jobs` is a `HashMap`, so `keys().next()` yields an arbitrary entry, and the code's own note says exactly that — *"Note mm_jobs is a HashMap, so the evicted entry is arbitrary, not FIFO - acceptable for a job cache since jobs expire naturally (submitted/current-height tracking)"*. That justification is recorded here rather than treated as compliance: since the row's proposition is FIFO, the row is not satisfied, it is *deviated from with a reason*. **And the same block contradicts itself one line up**: the header comment says *"Jobs older than the latest MAX_MM_JOBS entries are evicted"*, which is false for a HashMap and is the third comment-vs-code mismatch found in this campaign (with `OBL-C26`'s sled-batch claim and `OBL-C17`'s float/bulk-memory claim). The sibling structure `mm_jobs_submitted` uses the identical pattern (`:751-760`, also single-entry, also from an unordered container). **CLOSED 2026-09-23 by implementing the rule the spec and both comments already stated** — `merge-mining-ffi.md` §4.4 requires the oldest entry, so the direction was never in question. Both tables now carry an **insertion sequence** as their value (`mm_jobs`, `mm_jobs_submitted`: `HashMap<JobId, u64>`, fed by one `MiningState::mm_jobs_seq` so "oldest" means the same thing in each), and the eviction is one helper, `evict_oldest`, called by both sites. Nothing about the *shape* was invented: the sequence is the "order tracker alongside the container" the existing test already modelled by hand, moved into the container itself. The three comment-vs-code contradictions go with it: the header now says what happens, and the two branch comments that claimed FIFO while calling `iter().next()` no longer claim anything. **The tests are the finding worth recording**: `test_fifo_eviction_removes_oldest_not_newest` and `test_submitted_fifo_eviction` did **not** exercise the daemon's eviction at all — the first built its own `HashMap` + `Vec` pair and evicted from *them*, and the second removed from a local `HashSet` with the comment *"arbitrary pick from set"* and asserted only the resulting length. Both passed against the defect they are named after. They are **rewritten to call `evict_oldest`**, and to assert *which* entry goes, since asserting a length cannot distinguish FIFO from arbitrary. **Control and negative control**: they pass today, and with `keys().next()` restored as the picker they fail with `the OLDEST entry (job_000) must be the one evicted` and `the OLDEST submission must be the one evicted`, recorded verbatim (the arbitrary pick would have agreed with FIFO about once in 100 and once in 1000 respectively — the assertions could not be made absolute, so the odds are stated) |
| OBL-C56 | **PARTLY** | A miner does not mine during a `SYNC_BEHIND` transition (no sync-state TOCTOU) | `H-M12` | M | **PARTLY — the gate is real and re-checked every attempt; the check and the act are not atomic, and the residual window is bounded by the accept path, not eliminated. Read 2026-09-22.** The gate exists and is not a one-shot: `bin/dwowd/src/lib.rs:1412-1431` re-reads `sync_state` at the top of **each** mining iteration — `if state != SyncState::CaughtUp { …wait 1s; continue; }` — with the comment naming the purpose ("Avoids mining at a stale height when peers have advanced"), and the state is logged on transition so an operator sees why mining stopped instead of a silent spin. `Behind` is set by the consensus task on a crash (`:1080`, described there as terminal until restart) and the loop is also gated at startup (`:1387` waits for `CaughtUp`). What the row calls TOCTOU is nonetheless present in the narrow sense: `sync_state` is an `AtomicU8` (`:855`), so the read at the top of the iteration and the mining attempt that follows it are not one atomic step — a transition landing between them admits one attempt at a height that is already stale. That is bounded rather than closed: the attempt builds from local chain state and the resulting block is judged by `accept_block`'s own height/extension checks, so the worst case is a rejected block and a wasted nonce search, not a fork. Closing it properly would mean holding the state as a lease across the attempt, which the register should ask for explicitly rather than treat as implied by the atomic load. **The window is narrowed, and the lease is explicitly NOT taken — 2026-09-23.** So that this row's request is answered rather than left standing: a lease *cannot* be held across the attempt, because the attempt is a RandomX search that can run for minutes and the consensus task must stay free to declare the node Behind — a mining attempt that blocked that declaration would stall sync on the one transition it exists to detect. What is done instead is the closest thing that keeps the sync task unblocked: the miner **re-observes** the state at the last point where abandoning the block is still free, immediately before `accept_block`, sharing the recovery path with the existing post-mining "a peer block arrived at this height" check. A block mined during a transition is now discarded and its mempool transactions re-inserted, rather than proposed at a height the network has moved past; `take_competing_blocks` is not compensated on this path, which is the same behaviour that path already had. **What this does not claim**: the residual the row measures — a rejected block and a wasted nonce search when the transition lands *between* the re-check and acceptance — is unchanged, and `accept_block`'s own height and extension checks remain the thing that bounds it. No test covers it: the miner loop has no harness, and the change is in the loop body rather than in a callable unit, so the row records that rather than implying verification |

That third one is the row's concern and it holds: the comment records that the *previous* form was the real defect — a debug-only assertion meant debug and release behaved differently, with release recording an identity commitment as an uncle entry — and skipping is now defined behaviour in both profiles. The conflation is also unreachable, because the entries are filtered to `pin_accepted && pin_confirmed > 0` before the commitment is built (`:1087`) and the blind is a hash, so a validly-zero pin never reaches it. The cumulative chain's identity *value* remains a legitimate zero, not an absence |
| OBL-C58 | **SATISFIED** | A Pedersen chain integrity check exists | `H-M16` | M | **SATISFIED — the chain is checked at every step, in the contract and again in the host; only the standalone verifier does not carry the commitment half. Read 2026-09-22, evidence shared with `OBL-C3` and `OBL-C25`.** The integrity check exists in two places rather than one. In the contract, `pow_reward_v1` verifies the chain link by link: the prover's `old_cumulative_commit` must equal the on-chain value (`native_token/…/entrypoint/mod.rs:1105-1117`, with the blind checked too except at genesis), and `new_cumulative_commit` must equal `old_cumulative + pr.output.value_commit` (`:1122-1129`) — so a block cannot advance the Pedersen accumulator by any amount other than its own coinbase commitment. In the host, the same step is re-derived independently of the WASM overlay and the block is rejected on any disagreement (`block_acceptor.rs:656-689`, `OBL-C25`), which is what makes the check a cross-check rather than a mirror. What does **not** carry it is the only standalone verifier: `verify_cumulative_supply.sh` compares the stored plaintext total against the schedule and says so itself (*"Full Pedersen commitment chain verification … is demonstrated by the Python model"*, `:70-72`), and the RPC returns the stored entry unverified (`OBL-C45`). So the row's proposition holds; the caveat is about the tooling, not the enforcement |

### The finality widgets' residue (`OBL-C63`+)

DarkWow ships two finality layers — Caribina (Arweave-anchored) and the Monero anchoring gadget — and
asserts a 51% security property for each. Reading both end to end against the code that enforces them
produced this residue. The unifying shape is worth stating once, because it is what makes six rows out
of one design error: **finality is enforced from free header fields, while the verifying code that
would authenticate those fields exists and is never called.** `caribina::verify_anchor` is called only
from its own test file; `should_verify_anchor` and `should_verify_monero_anchor` have no production
caller anywhere; `verify_monero_anchor` is re-exported at `src/linear/src/lib.rs:103` and called by
nothing but its own tests; and `bin/dwowd/src/proto/linear_broadcast.rs` contains zero occurrences of
`anchor` or `finality`. The only live finality mechanism is the guard below, and it consults no proof.

Two rows — `C69` and `C70` — are not about finality at all despite being found here; they are the
merge-mining proof and the block-size bound, and they surfaced because reading this surface end to end
means reading `PowSource`. They are worth keeping adjacent to this residue rather than filed elsewhere:
`C69` is the merge-mining half of the same question ("what authenticates a block's claim about an
external chain?"), and it is the more severe of the two.

**A coverage gap found alongside them, now closed, recorded because it bears on how much these rows can
be trusted.** Merge mining's security argument is three receipts, and two of them had **no test in any
feature configuration**: `extract_aux_merkle_root` (Receipt 1) and `is_coinbase_valid_merkle_root` with
`check_coinbase_path` (Receipt 3) were reachable only from `validation.rs:82`, `block_acceptor.rs:194`
and `mm_rpc.rs:509`/`:561`. The one test that touched them, `test_monero_powdata_serde`, is
`#[cfg(feature = "async")]` and exercised them incidentally. Four tests were added on 2026-09-22:
Receipt 1 against the real merge-mined testnet block plus absent-tag and **two-tag ambiguity** controls
(the second matters because `mm_submit_solution` compares the submitted proof against the extracted root,
so a coinbase carrying two tags would let a submitter choose which to satisfy — the code refuses that,
and nothing had checked it); and Receipt 3 with a positive control on the real block plus two negatives
that attack its two halves separately. The positive control passing is itself a result: it establishes
that the coinbase-hash reconstruction — prefix keccak state, `tx_extra`, the null `RctSigBase` and a null
hash — is correct for a real Monero block, which nothing had verified.

| OBL-C63 | **CLOSED** | Finality is conferred by a *verified* anchor, not by a header field the relaying peer chooses. **CLOSED 2026-09-22 (`5c6bf01a7c`).** Both enforcement sites (`chain_state.rs:1011`, `:1546`) now require `caribina::verify_anchor_proof(&header)` — a pure local function, so consensus can call it — and share one predicate, so a block `connect_block` treats as un-replaceable cannot be one `detect_reorg` is willing to reorg away. The mirror direction the row insisted on holds: a block asserting an anchor it cannot prove confers **no** finality, and is deliberately not rejected either, because rejection would let any peer halt the chain with a malformed relay whereas ignoring the claim costs only that block's finality. That asymmetry is what removes the free chain-freeze. Proven by the positive control and the forged-key control in `chain_state::tests::test_finality_conferred_without_any_anchor_verification`, and the eight negatives in `caribina::verify::tests` | `chain_state.rs:1011`, `:1546`; `caribina/verify.rs` | C |

The four older fields (`anchor_tx_id`, `anchor_monero_*`, `finality_flags`) remain outside the blob, because they are set after the nonce and must not invalidate the solution they annotate — and they are no longer consulted for finality at all, so their malleability buys an attacker nothing. **Fixed on 2026-09-22, in the rows above.** `OBL-C71` — `DataItem::deserialize` now rejects a declared
tag area that does not fit the buffer (`checked_add`, so the near-`u64::MAX` case cannot overflow), and
the test that used to assert the panic is the regression control asserting rejection.
`OBL-C69` — `PowSource` gained a codec of its own (`src/linear/src/serial_sync.rs`) and `Serialize`/
`Deserialize` impls that carry *its* bytes, so serde and the canonical codec cannot disagree about the
field; the `skip` is gone and the fail-open `_ => PowSource::Native` arm is now an error.
`OBL-C70` — follows from `OBL-C69`: the acceptance measure now grows with the merge-mining proof.
`OBL-C68` — the Arweave POST in `stratum_submit` is made with `linear_submit_lock` released; the
behavioural test is the Stage 4 integration test the row names, since the lock scope is not observable
without a stub Turbo server. `OBL-C76` — recorded, not fixed: it describes a verification *practice*.

**Landed 2026-09-22: the anchor proof rides in the block, and enforcement verifies it.** This is the
consensus-format change the design constraint above requires, and it **moves the header hash** — the
mining blob grew 260 → 292 bytes for `anchor_owner`, and the genesis pin was re-recorded from
`e281afa8…` to `538b1634…` as a declared consequence, not a masked one.

- **`OBL-C63` — CLOSED.** Both enforcement sites (`chain_state.rs:1011`, `:1546`) now require
  `caribina::verify_anchor_proof(&header)`, a pure local function. A block whose anchor cannot be
  verified confers **no** finality, and — deliberately — is not rejected outright either: rejecting
  would let any peer halt the chain with a malformed relay, whereas ignoring the claim costs only that
  block's finality. That asymmetry is what removes the free chain-freeze. The old predicate read
  `anchor_tx_id != 0 || anchor_monero_height != 0`, two fields a relaying peer chooses.
- **`OBL-C64` — CLOSED for the field that matters.** `anchor_owner` (a fresh per-block Ed25519 key)
  is inside the mining blob, so a peer cannot re-attribute an anchor to a block it did not mine
  without redoing the proof-of-work. The four post-mining fields remain outside the preimage — they
  must, or anchoring would invalidate the solution it anchors — and they are no longer consulted for
  finality, so their malleability buys an attacker nothing.
- **`OBL-C65` — CLOSED by construction, and the wrong invariant deleted.** `should_verify_anchor` and
  `should_verify_monero_anchor` had no production caller and returned `false` whenever their
  `*_enabled` flag was off while `should_enforce` ignored those flags — a node could enforce what it
  had decided not to check. They are **removed** rather than corrected: a dead method encoding a wrong
  invariant is worse than no method, and "a verifier with no caller" is this campaign's root cause.
  Enforcement and verification are now literally the same call.
- **`OBL-C66` — recorded here as still open; superseded later the same day, and now
  ACCEPTED-WITH-REASON.** An anchor is *verified*; Arweave *settlement*
  is not checked at all. It cannot be a consensus rule — settlement lives on another chain and
  consensus must be a pure function of local data — so what remains is the node-local settle policy
  the row's fix note describes. Recorded as open rather than quietly implied to be done.
  **Correction (2026-09-22, after this paragraph was written):** that "node-local settle policy" is
  **not** written, and the row does not wait on one. What the proof establishes is **publication** —
  the miner committed a key in the block's mined region, signed a DataItem binding that block, and
  published it — and publication is the property the 51% argument uses, because the adversary in scope
  cannot delete a DataItem. Settlement depth is Arweave's business and this chain does not read it, so
  the gap between *settled* and *published* is **recorded in the row rather than narrowed**, and
  `caribina.md` no longer advertises a settlement time. The paragraph above is kept as the record of
  what was believed before that decision, not as a task.
- **`OBL-C67` — still open.** The Monero anchor is not yet derived from `MoneroPowData`, and the local
  Monero PoW check is not yet in place.
- **Anchoring is now real on both miner paths.** The RPC miner anchored in a detached task that never
  mutated the header, so every block it committed carried zeroed anchor fields; the built-in `miner_task`
  never anchored at all. Both now build the proof after the nonce and attach it **before**
  `accept_block`, and publish it asynchronously afterwards — publication is best-effort and, crucially,
  no longer the thing finality depends on. Merge-mined blocks commit no `anchor_owner`: they have no
  DarkWow preimage of their own to bind one into, so Caribina is unavailable to that path by
  construction rather than by omission.
- **Tests.** `verify_anchor_proof` carries a positive control plus eight negatives, one per condition
  (no proof, zero owner, foreign signer, another block's proof, altered height, altered timestamp,
  truncated bytes, and a `tag_bytes` overflow); `anchor_commitment` is asserted invariant under the
  post-mining fields and sensitive to the owner and nonce; `chain_state` carries a verified-anchor
  positive control beside a forged-key control, with the unanchored case as the baseline. The
  `OBL-C63` and `OBL-C64` characterization tests are flipped, and two blob-length assertions moved.

**A design constraint derived while fixing the above, recorded because it is not obvious and it
determines the shape of the remaining change.** The tempting cheap fix for `OBL-C63`/`OBL-C64` is to
require only that a *descendant* commit the block's `anchor_tx_id` in its mined region — no proof in
the block, no `anchor_owner`, nothing verified at the enforcement site, and the anchor becomes
PoW-authenticated transitively by the next block's work. **That fix is unsound, and not marginally.**
`anchor_tx_id` would then be 32 bytes the miner chooses, so any miner could finalize any block they
mined by asserting an id and committing it in the next block; after two blocks every block would be
un-replaceable and the chain could never reorganise at all. A finality rule needs an artefact the
claimer cannot produce unilaterally, or it degrades into "no reorgs, ever". So the anchor **proof** —
the signed ANS-104 DataItem, authored by a key committed in the block's mined region and binding the
anchor-zeroed header hash — must ride inside the block and be verified by a pure local function. That
is why the remaining work is a consensus-format change rather than a predicate tweak, and why it must
be verified before it lands: it moves the header hash.

**One further defect, recorded but not opened as a finality row.** `mm_get_aux_block` parses p2pool's
`address` parameter, logs a warning and ignores it (`mm_rpc.rs:178-190`), so the node mines to its own
declared key and a merge miner's DarkWow reward does not route to the address it asked for. That is a
reward-routing and economic defect, not a finality one, and folding it into this residue would bury it
under the wrong root cause; it wants its own row and its own plan. Until then it is pinned by a test so
it cannot drift silently.

**Process items, not obligations.** From the same corpus, and they belong with the three the register
already carries: `compile-fragilities` `A4`/`A5` (`-j 8` and `--test-threads 4` for heavy sweeps —
both are standing rules in the repository's memory, not open findings); `A6` (`--no-fail-fast` on
sweeps, and the `aws-lc-rs`/`ring` `--all-features` conflict that makes `quic_transport` abort a
sweep); `build-resource` `B7` (BuildKit, not configured — a deliberate future enhancement); and the
`hazop-darkleaf-in-contractcall-data` proposal, whose own verdict was **REJECT** and which was never
implemented — recorded as closed-by-rejection rather than left to look like untracked work.

### The contract phase rules — found by reading the genesis contracts as a benchmark (`OBL-C72`+)

The nine genesis contracts were read end to end, not sampled, and set against the other 25. They
observe two rules **without exception**, and three of them state the rule in a comment:
`native_token/src/entrypoint/mod.rs:1405-1407` ("Exec computed the running total; Apply only writes
it — no read in Apply — db_get ACL excludes Update"), `box/src/entrypoint/mod.rs:143-144`, and
`purse/src/entrypoint/mod.rs:202`. Both rules are normative in
[contract-wasm-type-system.md](../arch/contract-wasm-type-system.md) §A.4.7 and §B.2.2 and enforced
mechanically by the host ACL. **Neither has a register row, a checklist line, or a gate script** —
`grep -rln "ContractSection\|acl_allow\|read triad" scripts/ script/*.py hooks/` returns nothing, and
no script in the repository references the ACL section model at all.

That absence is the finding, and it is what makes these rows worth separating from `OBL-C1`–`C71`.
Every other rule in this repository that *has* a gate — domain separation, instance derivation,
metadata alignment, pubkey binding — appears in this register as measured and is wholly or partly
closed. These two had none, and drifted to **86 violations across 12 contracts, none of them genesis**.

The measurement is `scripts/check-phase-host-functions.sh`, which parses each contract's declared
`define_contract!` entrypoints, builds the call closure from `exec` and `apply`, and takes the
permitted sections from the `acl_allow` call sites in `src/runtime/import/*.rs` **at run time** — so
the gate cannot drift from the ACL it checks, the RC5 failure this repository has had four times.
**The gate corrected this row's first draft**: an earlier ad-hoc scan reported 66 sites and missed
`insurance_market` entirely (15 sites — its apply handlers are `*_process_update_v1` in per-function
files, which a name-pattern scan does not match) and the read-only getters `get_verifying_block_height`
(four sites) and `get_call_index` (one), whose ACLs also exclude `Update`. The 86 is the gate's
number; 66 was a pattern-matching artifact.

**Re-measured 2026-09-23, and both of those numbers are now stale in the same direction.** The gate
reports **7 violations, in one contract**, all one class:

```
$ bash scripts/check-phase-host-functions.sh ; echo EXIT=$?
FAIL: src/contract/drain_protection/src/entrypoint.rs:368: init_fund_process_instruction_v1() -> db_set()  (legal in ('Deploy', 'Update'))
       … (the same shape at :439, :491, :542, :600, :630, :662 — seven sites, all drain_protection)
FAIL: 7 phase violation(s).
EXIT=1
```

So **read-in-apply is at 0 sites everywhere** — `OBL-C72`'s rule now holds without exception — and
**write-in-exec is at 7, all in `drain_protection`**. Two corrections follow from the same run: the
**86** above and the *script's own docstring* (`check-phase-host-functions.sh:20`, "66 sites across
11 non-genesis contracts") are both stale self-descriptions of a family that has moved; and the
seven survivors are the residue of a contract whose state cannot commit at all — its `process_update`
is a no-op (`drain_protection/src/entrypoint.rs:791-794`, `Ok(())` with the update discarded), so the
exec-phase `db_set` is the *only* write path and every transition fails the ACL. That is `OBL-C73`'s
proposition measured false, and it is recorded there rather than here.

**And the gate that found this is not wired into `run-all-tests.sh`.** Its `run_gate` list (lines
76-146) has no `check-phase-host-functions` entry, so seven live violations cannot fail a full run —
which is the same "a gate nobody runs" shape this family's own filing text names, one level up.

**Corrected 2026-09-23: it is wired, as a ratchet.** `run-all-tests.sh` now runs
`exec/apply phase rule` with the static audits, and `scripts/check-phase-host-functions.sh` takes
its seven known sites from `script/phase_host_function_exceptions.txt` (content-keyed on
`<file> : <fn>() -> <host>()` rather than on line numbers, following
`script/circuit_free_instances.txt`), printing each as `EXCEPTED` with the register ID that
schedules it and exiting 0 while a *new* violation still exits 1. Negative-controlled both ways
before wiring: with the exception file removed the gate exits 1 with all seven, and with one entry
dropped it exits 1 naming exactly that site — so the exceptions are demonstrably what suppresses
the findings rather than a bug in the filter. The paragraph above is kept as the record of what
was true when the row was filed; what it named as the gap is now the mechanism that closes it.

| OBL-C120 | **FIXED** | No node relays or accepts a block whose timestamp lies beyond a bounded interval ahead of local time — the relay policy the code says it has | `src/linear/src/validation.rs` (`check_future_timestamp`, `MAX_FUTURE_SECS`) — applied at **both** entry points: `bin/dwowd/src/proto/linear_broadcast.rs` (the relay) and `bin/dwowd/src/task/consensus_linear.rs` (the sync loop) | found 2026-09-24 while correcting `OBL-C110`'s specification | M | **NEW 2026-09-24: a claim of enforcement with no enforcement behind it — the `OBL-C111` species, found by grepping for the thing being cited, which is the check the doc comment's own assertion was never given.** The comment read "The future-timestamp check (Bitcoin Core's MAX_FUTURE) is a network policy, not a consensus rule. The only rule on a timestamp anywhere is `check_block_timestamp`'s median check, which is a *lower* bound. **What an unbounded future timestamp costs, read from the retarget rather than asserted:** `compute_adjustment` (`src/linear/src/consensus.rs:483-543`) takes the last 10 timestamps, sums the 9 intervals between them, and **abandons the adjustment outright when any interval is negative** (`:499-505`, the `OBL-C37` guard, whose own comment says why a fabricated interval must not be manufactured). A block dated far ahead makes every window containing it abort, because the next block's interval into it is negative, so **one miner, with one block and no extra hashrate, freezes difficulty adjustment for up to 10 blocks** — and the median rule cannot see it, since a future timestamp is above the median by construction. The sharper direction needs a window rather than a block: a party holding the last 10 timestamps moves `avg_interval` and drives the target up to 10% per block (`:526-542`) toward `min_target` or `max_target`. **Why M and not H**: the free effect is a *freeze*, which mints nothing by itself, and the paying direction — easier mining — still requires the majority of a 10-block window, the same premise the finality rows already price. **What would close it**: a relay-layer bound (Bitcoin Core's two hours) as a **node-local policy, never a consensus rule** — the reason the row above gives, and the shape `OBL-C67`'s monerod confirmation depth already takes, since a predicate reading the local clock is not a function of block data (`type-system.md` §9). Until it exists the comment may not claim it; **that half is corrected today**, in the same change as `OBL-C110`'s **PARTLY 2026-10-08: the broadcast path is bounded, the sync path is not — and the row's own "what would close it" is what was built.** `check_future_timestamp(timestamp, local_now, max_future_secs)` and `MAX_FUTURE_SECS` (two hours, Bitcoin Core's constant) live in `src/linear/src/validation.rs` beside the median rule, so the lower and upper bounds on this field are read together; **`local_now` is a parameter rather than a call to the clock**, which keeps the predicate a pure function of its inputs — the discipline the rest of that module holds — and makes the boundary testable. It is wired in `bin/dwowd/src/proto/linear_broadcast.rs`'s `handle_receive_block`, beside the existing height-gap rejection and for the same reasons (cheap, and before the RandomX VM is built): a broadcast block more than two hours ahead of the local clock is logged and skipped, never relayed onward. **A node-local policy and not a consensus rule, which is why it is not in `check_block_header`**: the clock is read at exactly one call site, the relay one. **Two tests, both passing** (`cargo test --release -p dwow_chain --features pow future_` → `2 passed`): the three places a bound can be wrong (inside, exactly at, one second beyond — the middle asserted because the comparison is `>` and a fixture that skipped it would accept `>=`), and the property that makes this a policy rather than a rule — *the same block becomes admissible one second later*, which no consensus predicate may do. **Arm (a) is CLOSED 2026-10-08; the row stays PARTLY for arm (b), which is a decision.** The relay path already refused to forward such a block — `linear_broadcast.rs`, before the RandomX VM. The **sync path now refuses to accept one**: `bin/dwowd/src/task/consensus_linear.rs` applies the same `check_future_timestamp` beside its proof-of-token-balance pre-filter, before the VM for the same reason the relay path puts it there, and scores the peer like a PoTB failure — a peer serving a block no node will accept is the peer's problem, not a local one. `check_block_timestamp`'s doc comment said *"No such policy is implemented in this tree"*, true only until the relay half landed; it now names both entry points. **What keeps this at PARTLY**: arm (b), a node's **own** mined block. The residual is named rather than left as a TODO, and the row closes with both entry points bounded. |

Two things were learned on the way and are recorded here rather than in the commit alone. **First, why a comment is a pin-mover at all**: `src/sdk/src/**` file *line numbers* live in the contract wasm — a panic `Location` records `file:line` — so inserting five lines into `capability.rs` shifts whatever locations point into it, and the bytes move even though no behaviour changed. That is the mechanism behind the other session's `-Zlocation-detail=none` work, met here from the other side: it is why this row needed the batch rather than a drive-by, and it is checkable rather than assumed. **Second, the batch it rode:** `attestation` gained `CheckAttestationV1` (0x0d) so `labor_market/create_job`'s `attestation_id` has a callee that reverts on an unknown or inactive id, the contract was rebuilt clean, and the genesis pin was re-recorded from the ceremony's own value — `c8afdeb73f2c9f29839a0761b585beaccc7407b5bcf008bf9fbcaf992e166d9b`, replacing `c43ae8c36fa89f0807b5520d6ff7c7bb22187a243cac747ef4360d274c34a0c7`, with `genesis_pin_is_current` and `genesis_pin_rejects_a_wrong_hash` both green afterwards |

It is wired into `run-all-tests.sh`, and it is deliberately shallow: an arm returning a *variable* is out of scope, because a shape check that tried to follow values is the cleverer classifier this register has twice rejected. **Found while doing this, and fixed in the same commit**: the `relayer` feature configuration **did not compile at all** — `src/relayer.rs:258` used `SerializedLen` without importing it — so the three gated instructions had never been built in any configuration, and my new arms for them could not be verified until it did. A half-built lock, and the half that is missing is the side that would check it. *Why this is M and not C or H, stated as the path that fails rather than as an assurance.* For a withdraw to be accepted the prover must reproduce `old_leaf` and a merkle path to the exposed `expected_root`, which requires `old_balance` and `state_nonce`. Both are private to the owner's wallet and appear on chain only inside a Pedersen commitment (`new_commit_x/y`) and a leaf hash, so an attacker without them cannot build the path — which means the search for a path from untrusted input to stolen funds fails *at the same gate the vacuous check would have failed at*. So there is no demonstrated harm, and this register does not rank an undemonstrated one. What the missing check costs is the second lock: **if the leaf preimage ever leaks — a wallet bug, a log, a backup — nothing else stands between the holder of those two field elements and the balance**, and the `owner_commit` that was supposed to be that lock is inert. Recorded so the next reader does not start from a comparison whose right-hand side does not exist **CLOSED 2026-09-25, by the leaf-binding fix, and the severity moved with it: `M` → `C`.** The row's own severity argument rested on a conditional — *"the merkle-leaf preimage is the only real gate, so **a leak of it** is what the missing check would backstop … if the leaf preimage ever leaks — a wallet bug, a log, a backup"* — and an external reading of this chain (`github.com/9lordisgod/DarkWow-Chain-Research`, finding 8, 2026-09-24) removed the condition: `PutParams`/`DepositParams`/`WithdrawParams` carry the leaf preimage ingredients **in plaintext**, and the transaction hash commits to every byte of the call data, so the preimage is not something that might leak — it is published by the creating transaction. As an unfixed defect this was therefore theft of a purse's balance, not a latent weakness, and the severity is corrected rather than left at the value its own reasoning does not support. **The repair took a different route than this row prescribed, and the row's prescription is the weaker one.** It said "wire the purse record, then bind against it"; `owner_pub` is now folded into the **leaf** (`deposit.zk:57,93`, `withdraw.zk:63,97`, `balance.zk:47`), so the spender's secret is pinned by the value the tree stores rather than by a record. That is strictly stronger: binding against a stored record stops a stranger but not the legitimate owner, who could still spend one leaf twice with two secrets — both spends publishing the same owner value and *different* nullifiers, which the chain's de-duplication cannot see. The leaf binding admits one nullifier per leaf, so the same mechanism closes both halves. **What the row's `owner_commit` clause still names is now a different question**: the record remains unwired, so there is no on-chain association between a purse and its owner for *deduplication* or *privacy* purposes — an authorization repair no longer needed, and a deduplication/privacy item still open. The two exception-list entries this row carried (`deposit.zk`, `withdraw.zk`) moved from defect-named to arm (b) transitive in the same pass, which is what `script/circuit_pubkey_binding_exceptions.txt`'s header records. |

The finding is external and stated plainly: `put.zk`/`take.zk` computed `leaf = H(5, box_id, contents, nonce)` with **no owner term**, while the nullifier is `H(1, owner_secret, box_id, nonce)` and `owner_secret` appeared in exactly one constraint — so consumption authority was knowledge of the leaf preimage, which the params publish, and one leaf admitted one valid nullifier *per distinct secret*, which block-level de-duplication cannot see because the nullifiers genuinely differ. Nothing on the host compensated: `exec` checked an unspent nullifier and a historical root and nothing else, no contract stored an owner, the registry is a bare `BTreeSet<Nullifier>`, no owner reached any public input, and no test would have caught it — the harness hard-codes `os = 42` on every box and purse operation. **The repair implements the specification rather than changing it**: `box.md:25` already listed the barb — `owner_pub == poseidon_hash(DOMAIN_SIGNATURE_SECRET, owner_secret)` — that no circuit contained. | OBL-C92 | **DECISION** | A redemption releases the collateral it claims, and the pool's ledger is written down only against debt that existed | `stablecoin/src/entrypoint.rs:1657-1658`, `:1694-1707`, `:1711-1727`; `stablecoin/src/model/mod.rs:985-988`; `promissory_note/proof/redeem.zk:50,53-55`; `promissory_note/proof/revoke.zk:70-72`; `promissory_note/src/entrypoint/mod.rs:1052-1057`, `:1070-1088` | **NEW 2026-09-23, found by the payout read `OBL-C82` held its severity open for.** That row asked *who funds the child transfer that pays the liquidator*; this is the third arm of the same contract, and the one where the ledger moves with no transfer asked for at all. *Both sides read, in one pass.* **The parent** (`process_redeem_stable_instruction`): it decodes the child, requires it to be `promissory_note::redeem_v1` (0x01) targeting PN, and then reads the child's output **only** for `spend_hook` (`:1660-1669`) — the value commits `validate_child_redeem_v1` returns are bound to `_receipt_value_commit`/`_receipt_token_commit` and discarded (`:1657-1658`). The payout it credits is `collateral_return = params.redeem_amount * total_collateral / total_debt` (`:1699-1704`), computed from the config DB and a **caller-chosen parameter**, bound only by `params.redeem_amount <= total_debt` (`:1694-1697`). The struct's own `total_debt` / `total_collateral`, documented *"Current total debt/collateral before redemption"* (`model/mod.rs:985-988`), are compared to the stored values **nowhere** — `params.total_debt` appears only in the log at `:1629` and inside the replay guard's hash (`:1714`), and `params.total_collateral` only in the log. **The child** (`promissory_note::redeem_v1`): merkle root exists, nullifier unspent, receipt commitment unique (`:1070-1088`) — and conservation is *deliberately absent* (`:1052-1057`: *"Redemption IS value destruction ... Value conservation is deliberately NOT enforced here"*). What the redemption actually pays is the receipt coin, and `redeem.zk` pins it to zero on both sides: `constrain_instance(value)` (`:50`) and `constrain_equal_base(value, ZERO)` (`:53-55`). *So the proposition is unenforced on both sides, and the payout is nothing.* The collateral release the property names is implemented **neither** in the child (a zero-value receipt) **nor** in the parent (which never binds `collateral_return` to anything the child moved). What a call does instead is write the pool's ledger down by an amount its caller chooses, up to `total_debt`, against a note of *any* value: the redeem input must be a real note — its `Revoke_V2` proof constrains merkle inclusion (`revoke.zk:70-72`) — but nothing binds that note's value to `redeem_amount`, and the "unique nullifier" `poseidon_hash([redeem_amount, asset_id, params.total_debt])` (`:1711-1715`) is built entirely of caller-chosen values, so it forbids an identical repeat and nothing else. *Why H and not C.* No value is minted, destroyed or stolen: the payer receives a receipt that is zero by circuit, and the collateral notes are untouched — they stay in the PN commitment set, spendable only by the holder of their `spend_secret`, and no arm of this contract can move one without it. What is destroyed is the **record** of what the pool owes, which is exactly the ledger `OBL-C82`'s `total_debt` and this `total_collateral` compose and which two consumers read (`:1701`, `:1279`): a stated safety property broken, not a value transfer. *The repair is two-sided, and the same shape as `OBL-C82`'s in the same order*: the child redeem must carry the collateral output the parent pays; the circuit must instance the input's `value_commit` so the parent can compare Pedersen sums against `collateral_return`; and the parent must then bind `collateral_return` to the burned value rather than to the ledger. *Not repaired here, for `OBL-C83`'s reason and one more*: `stablecoin/src/client/` holds **no redeem client** — its eight entries are `accrue_interest`, `governance_report`, `initialize`, `liquidate`, `mint_stable`, `mod`, `open_position`, `zkbins` — so there is no working flow to repair against, only a contract-side claim. Stablecoin is not genesis, so nothing here moves the pin | H |

| OBL-C93 | **CLOSED** | A node's shipped default configuration is one the node can actually load | `bin/dwowd/dwowd_config.toml` (`include_str!` into the binary, `main.rs:46`); `src/util/cli.rs:151-170` (write-then-reparse on first run); `bin/dwowd/src/main.rs:119` (`create_genesis: bool`, required) | no gate runner examines the template; measured by hand 2026-09-23 with `HOME`/`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` redirected to a scratch directory | M | **NEW 2026-09-23, found while verifying `OBL-C80`'s fix, and it is the failure that came first.** `BlockchainNetwork.create_genesis` is a required field (`main.rs:119` — a plain `bool` in a `#[structopt(long)]` with no `default_value`), and the shipped template carried it in **no** network section: `grep -c create_genesis bin/dwowd/dwowd_config.toml` → 0, and `git log -S create_genesis -- bin/dwowd/dwowd_config.toml` returns no commit at all, so the field was never there rather than removed by one. *Measured both ways.* A fresh `HOME` runs `dwowd` once, which writes the template and exits 2 with *"Config file created in … Please review it and try again."* (the documented first-run step); the **second** run — the shipped default, exactly as the operator was told to make it — then failed `ParseFailed("Failed parsing requested network configuration")` with *"missing field `create_genesis` at line 42 column 1"*, before any merge-mining or finality check could be reached. That is why `OBL-C80`'s consequence (i) was right about the conclusion and wrong about the cause: the node does not start, but not because of the `mm_rpc` gate. **Fixed here** by declaring `create_genesis = false` in the two *selectable* networks, `darkwow-devnet` and `darkwow-testnet` — the only two `main.rs:155-163` accepts, so the other three sections are unreachable and were left alone rather than given a field nothing parses. `--role genesis` / `CREATE_GENESIS=true` still overrides the value (`main.rs:276-280`), which is what leaves exactly one node per network able to run the ceremony. *Control, run on the shipped path rather than on a hand-built file*: with a binary rebuilt from this tree and `HOME`+`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` pointed at an empty directory, run 1 writes the template (`create_genesis` present, `mm_rpc` commented out) and run 2 reaches `Initializing a DarkWow daemon...`, failing only on `NODE_NAME not set` — the documented operational input, not a parse. Appending an `mm_rpc` section to that same written file makes it refuse with `merge mining requires monerod_url`, so the section is really parsed and the `OBL-C80` gate really bites |

| OBL-C94 | **CLOSED** | A log line names the network the node actually selected | `bin/dwowd/src/lib.rs:802` (`Dwowd::init_linear`) | measured 2026-09-23; `grep -rn "Initializing a DarkWow daemon" contrib/ scripts/ bin/` returns the source line and no consumer | M | **NEW 2026-09-23, found while controlling `OBL-C93`: a claim the log made that was not true.** `init_linear` logged `Initializing a DarkWow daemon for darkwow-devnet...` as a **literal**, so a node selected as `darkwow-testnet` announced itself as devnet. | OBL-C96 | **DECISION** | A milestone's payment is the amount the job records for that milestone, and a completed job's releases reconcile with the job's total | `labor_market/src/entrypoint.rs:1507-1522`, `:1514`; `labor_market/src/model/mod.rs:56-67` (`Milestone.payment_amount`), `:200` (`Job.released_payment`) | found by the `OBL-Z16` triage of `milestone_payment.zk`, in the same read that declared the circuit's instance safe; `labor_market`'s `confirm_milestone` arm read on both sides | M | **NEW 2026-09-23, and it is what is left after the circuit's half was found sound.** *Both sides, one pass.* The circuit's exposed `milestone_payment_amount` is forced to equal `params.payment_release` — the metadata arm publishes it (`entrypoint.rs:389`) and the runtime hands that vector to `verify_zkp` as the proof's public inputs (`src/linear/src/zk_verifier.rs:234-238`) — and `confirm_milestone_v1` binds the same params value to the child `promissory_note::transfer_v1` (`:1467-1472`). So the **transfer** is honest about what it pays. What is not compared is the **record**. The amount the job declares for the milestone is stored per-milestone at creation (`Milestone.payment_amount`, `model/mod.rs:60`) and read **nowhere**: every `milestones[...]` access in the host is `.completed` (`:1405`, `:1507` read, `:1512-1513` write), and every `payment_amount` the host consults is the *job-level* one (`job.payment_amount` at `:892`, `:1081`, `:1169`; `params.payment_amount` at creation). So `confirm_milestone_v1` marks the milestone complete and adds a caller-chosen amount to `released_payment` (`:1514`) with neither half of the reconciliation performed: the amount paid need not be the milestone's recorded amount, and when the last milestone completes the job is set `Confirmed` (`:1516-1522`) with `released_payment` never compared against `job.payment_amount` — that field is written and never read as a condition anywhere in the crate. *Why this is a record finding and not a value one.* No value is minted, destroyed or stolen: the child transfer is bound to the amount and draws on notes the transaction already owns, so a payer can only under- or over-pay out of its own pocket. What breaks is a stated property — the job record is the worker's and any arbiter's evidence of what was owed and what was paid, and "milestone N completed" is asserted against a figure the contract never consults. Severity M on the register's bar, which asks for a path from an untrusted input to value and finds none here. *The repair is one comparison, and which comparison is a decision rather than a reading*: either `confirm_milestone_v1` requires `params.payment_release == job.milestones[index].payment_amount`, rejecting partial payments, or it requires the accumulated `released_payment` to reach `job.payment_amount` before the job may be `Confirmed`. Both halves are half-written in the code, so the contract's intended model cannot be read off it, and this row records the finding rather than choosing one. **RESOLVED 2026-10-08 — the choice was a false dichotomy and the root cause was nowhere in the cell.** Both named repairs are symptoms of one unread field and one unenforced invariant, and two sibling endpoints show what the arm was meant to do: `refund_v1` already refuses a caller-chosen amount that differs from `job.payment_amount` (`entrypoint.rs:1176-1179`). · **The stored figure is read now.** `confirm_milestone_v1` requires `params.payment_release == job.milestones[params.milestone_index].payment_amount` (`:1686-1691`), refusing with the already-declared `InvalidMilestonePaymentAmount` (`Custom(24)`) — the variant `refund_v1` uses for exactly this comparison. Before it, the amount was the caller's to pick: `milestone_payment.zk` constrains `milestone_payment_amount` by a 64-bit `range_check` and an equality with a public input the metadata arm fills from the *same param* (`:401-427`), so the circuit never sees the job record, and the worker — who read `Milestone.payment_amount` before accepting — was paid a number the employer chose at payout. · **The invariant is enforced now.** `validate_milestone_total` (`model/mod.rs:112-123`) requires `params.payment_amount` to equal the milestones' sum, on both creation paths (`:1464`, `:2041`) — the invariant asserted in **two** places that checked it in none: `create_job_with_milestones_v1`'s comment ("a milestone job's `payment_amount` is what its milestones sum to") and the field's own doc (`model/mod.rs:1215`, "Total payment amount (sum of all milestones)"). `checked_add`, not `+`: the workspace sets no `overflow-checks`, so a silent wrap could have made a wrapped total satisfy the test. · **One field that looks inert here and is not, recorded because the reading cost it.** `CreateJobWithMilestonesParamsV1::milestone_count` is read nowhere in this entrypoint — the same shape as `OBL-C166`'s `claim_id` — and it is the *decoder's* loop bound (`model/mod.rs:1323-1334`), with `pos != data.len()` refused after the loop, so a count that disagrees with the vector cannot survive a successful decode. No finding, and a reminder that the host is one side of a pair. · The two together make `released_payment` reach `job.payment_amount` at the last confirmation, and make the `+=` at `:1698` non-wrapping by construction rather than by hope. · **What is NOT closed here, and why the status does not move.** The proposition's second half — a *completed* job's releases reconcile with the job's total — still fails, and its cause is not this endpoint. `submit_deliverable.zk` derives `spent_nullifier = poseidon_hash(DOMAIN_NULLIFIER, SUBMIT_TAG, job_id, worker_secret)`: job-and-worker keyed, not milestone-keyed. So the canonical client submits once per job, a confirmation returns the job to `InProgress` and nothing returns it to `Delivered`, and a job with more than one milestone can reach `Confirmed` only by confirming the **last** index in the single confirmation it gets — leaving its predecessors uncompleted and `released_payment` at that one milestone's amount. That is the shared-nullifier defect the file names above `confirm_delivery_v1` (HIGH-4), and the ordering asymmetry it forces — `submit_milestone_v1` requires `index == current_milestone` (`:1562-1565`), `confirm_milestone_v1` must not — is now written at the site (`:1665-1677`) so the next reader does not "fix" it and deadlock every multi-milestone job. The repair is a per-milestone nullifier in `milestone_payment.zk`: a circuit change, filed with the wire batch, and `DECISION` is this vocabulary's slot for filed wire work — as `OBL-C89`, `C146`, `C171` and `C203` all carry. Whether the *domain tags* themselves are prover-parametrisable (`DOMAIN_NULLIFIER` and `SUBMIT_TAG` are witness slots the circuit does not bind) is not settled here; that is `OBL-Z3`'s and `OBL-Z23`'s question and it is left to them. · **The negative result, recorded because it cost the reading.** The first attempt at this row added the ordering check to `confirm_milestone_v1` — the obvious half-pair repair, the shape `submit_milestone_v1` has and this lacks — and it is wrong: it makes a multi-milestone job uncompletable, because the one confirmation a job gets could then only name index 0. Reading the second side is what showed it, and the fixture already documented the asymmetry as deliberate (`labor_market_spec.rs`) without saying why. · **The control this row needed, and the trap it was found through.** `validate_milestone_total` is the whole of the sum check, so its five controls are direct (`src/contract/labor_market/tests/integration.rs`), covering the match, the mismatch, the overflow and the refusal's declared variant (`Custom(24)`); `confirm_milestone_v1`'s amount comparison has no counterpart there, because it is an `if` inside a handler that needs a job record, and its endpoint-level control is owed **with** the fixture blocker rather than after it — `OBL-C170` for the coverage bound, `OBL-C198` for the cause, which is that row's composition red and not anything in this contract. Writing the first of those controls is how a tree-wide trap surfaced: a `#[cfg(test)] mod` inside `entrypoint.rs` compiles to nothing in this crate and reports a green `0 passed`, recorded as its own row (`OBL-C208`). *What the five controls do not establish*: that the two call sites reach the helper, or that an endpoint refuses a mismatched call end to end. **BOTH POSITIVE HALVES NOW EXERCISED ON A CHAIN, 2026-10-08.** `test_heavyweight_labor_market` (1038.56s, log `/tmp/lm-att.log`) reaches local height 45 of 46 and passes both rows this change touches, with the contract's own log as the evidence: `[labor_market::confirm_milestone_v1] ZK proof verified, milestone confirmed, payment released: 1000` — job `0x…66`, release equal to `milestones[1].payment_amount`, admitted by the new comparison — and `CreateJobWithMilestonesV1` before it, whose `payment_amount` of 2000 is the sum of its two 1000s. So the sum check's two call sites are reached and accept a conforming call, and the amount comparison is reached and admits the recorded figure, each inside a frame carrying a second child. **What this still does not establish**: the *negative* half of either control at the endpoint — no row yet submits a create whose milestones do not sum, or a confirm whose release differs from the record, so neither refusal has been observed. The fixture now reaches those rows, which is what makes that the next cheap step rather than a fixture project. **BOTH CONTROLS NOW EXERCISED — the negative halves are measured, 2026-10-08.** `test_heavyweight_labor_market` (1074.74s, log `/tmp/lm-ctl2.log`) carries two new rows and both fired with the declared code: at local height 41 `call_idx=1 … ContractError(Custom(24))` for `CreateJobWithMilestonesV1_SumMismatch` (milestones summing to 1000 against `payment_amount` 2000, the same legal deposit child as the row below it, so the sum comparison is the only thing that could refuse), and at local height 44 the same `Custom(24)` for `ConfirmMilestoneV1_WrongAmount` (a release of `MILESTONE_PAYMENT + 1` against a record of `MILESTONE_PAYMENT`, with a note issued at `+ 1` so the *transfer* is legal). Both rows are `RejectionByEndpoint`, which asserts the **refuser's contract id** as well as the needle: a `RejectionNaming` needle could have been satisfied by the child, and the control would then have proved nothing. So the row's two checks are now measured in **both** directions on a chain — admitted when conforming, refused when not. **The first of the two was wrong when first written and the failure taught the contract something worth keeping**: it carried an `attestation_child` sibling, and `create_job_with_milestones_v1` refuses two children with `InvalidChildrenIndexes` (`Custom(31)`) *before* the sum comparison — the milestone create requires **exactly one** child where `create_job_v1` requires two, and the recorded refusal (`Custom(31)` at `call_idx=2`) is what identified it. **Still open, unchanged**: the proposition's second half — a completed job's releases reconciling with its total — is filed on a per-milestone nullifier, and the fixture's last row still dies on `FinalizeV2` (`OBL-C170`/`OBL-C198`), which is upstream of nothing here but is why the suite as a whole is red. **AND THE SUITE AROUND THEM IS NOW GREEN, 2026-10-08.** `test_heavyweight_labor_market` — `ok`, `1 passed; 0 failed`, 1989.39s, `EXIT=0` (`/tmp/lm-3lvl.log`) — so both checks are exercised inside a passing fixture rather than in a run that dies later, which is the strongest form of the evidence above: the two refusals at heights 41 and 44 are *expected* rejections the runner asserts, and every row after them passes. |

The process arms validate that the fund exists, that it is not locked, and that the rate limit holds — never who is calling. *The consequence, walked rather than asserted, because this register does not rank a value path it has not walked.* No arm of this contract moves value: `apply_transfer_update` only *records* the transfer (`:1007-1008`) and the child it requires is a `promissory_note::transfer_v1`, whose inputs each carry their own `Revoke_V2` proof and are therefore the **caller's own notes** (the read `OBL-C82` records), and the contract has no spend hook (`grep spend_hook` over the crate returns nothing). The stated safety property — only the authority may spend a protected fund — is therefore not enforced, which is `H` on this register's legend; it is not `C` because the value path above is bounded one layer down. *The fix is `OBL-C82`'s shape and was not taken here*: the host half compares the params' point against `fund.spend_authority` in each arm that holds a fund (`transfer`, `lock`, `unlock`, `update_config`, and `initialize` against the authority it registers), and the arms without one — `propose`, `vote`, `execute` — need the proposal-to-fund binding read first, which `OBL-C98` puts in the same place. The fixture is already written to match (`test-harness/src/harness/drain_protection.rs`: one authority secret, and `initialize` registers its point), so adding the check does not require rewriting it **PARTLY 2026-09-24: the five arms that hold a fund now compare, with a control that is a pair, and the residual is the arms that hold no fund.** *What landed.* `require_fund_authority` (`entrypoint.rs`, above `propose_process_instruction_v1`) compares the proof's `authority_pub_x/y` against `fund.spend_authority`'s point, refusing with `InvalidSpendAuthority` and naming the mismatch in a log line; it is called in `transfer`, `lock`, `unlock` and `update_config`, each immediately after the fund is decoded, and `initialize` gets the same comparison against the authority it is about to register (the fund does not exist yet, so both halves come from the call — the point the circuit derives and the point being registered, which is what keeps a creator from naming an authority it cannot use). The pair sits immediately after `initialize` in the spec, before the proposal flow, so both halves run before the run's later failure. *The residual, stated.* `propose`, `vote` and `execute` hold no fund — their arms look the fund up by a **proposal** or **multisig** id (`OBL-C98`), which is the same missing binding seen from the other side — and `exit`'s circuit instances only the tx pair, so its authorization cannot come from the proof at all: its witnesses for DAO membership are declared and its circuit block never reads them. Re-counting the threshold here would be a second source of truth that could disagree with the first. *The message is the proposal id, not the proposal's message hash* — `proposal_id = poseidon_hash([fund.id, message_hash])` — which is what binds an approval to one fund: an approval to execute fund A's proposal cannot be replayed as fund B's approval of the same action. *Executing now does something in this contract*: `apply_execute_update` writes the proposal id into the proposals tree — the first writer that tree has ever had — and the exec phase reads it to refuse a second execution, which is reachable because a group may legitimately approve the same proposal again with fresh signatures (the first approval's nullifiers are spent, so the second finalize needs new ones). `ExecuteUpdateV1` lost the `action` field it carried beside the id, assigned `params.proposal_id` at its only construction site and read nowhere. *And the record has a reader*: a rate-limited transfer used to require only that *some* proposal id was supplied — any id, including one nobody proposed. It now requires the proposal to have been **executed** (`db_contains_key(proposals_db, …)`), so "this transfer was approved" and "this transfer names an approval" are one fact rather than two. *Measured, in the contract's own logs*: `[ExecuteV1::apply] Proposal recorded as executed` for the accepted execution; `[ExecuteV1] Error: the approval is a different group's, not the fund's`; `[ExecuteV1] Error: the approval names a different proposal`; and `test_heavyweight_drain_protection` **ok** (543s), the setup creating the governance group on chain — three members, threshold two, the multisig contract's own `derive_group_id` called rather than re-implemented — and the fund registering it. *Three controls, each a valid approval the fund must refuse, and each able to fail*: `execute_foreign_group` has a **second** group (one member, threshold one) genuinely approve the same proposal, so the child commits and only the fund-versus-child group comparison stops it; `execute_foreign_message` has the fund's **own** group approve a different message, so again only the message comparison stops it; and `transfer_unexecuted_proposal` is the same transfer call with the same proof naming a proposal the fund's own group **approved** and nobody executed — the pair that distinguishes approved from executed. Remove any of the three checks and its endpoint starts succeeding. *Residual, stated rather than implied*: the proposal's message hash stays opaque — this contract has no action enum, so an execution's effect is the approval being spent plus the record, not a described action carried out, and a model where an execution carries validated children (as `ExitV1` and `TransferV1` validate theirs) is a further decision rather than a silent gap in this row. |
